title: How to avoid MLS fines by correcting listing data errors on a Mac in 2026
metaTitle: Avoid MLS Fines by Correcting Listing Data Errors | Lazur
description: Learn what MLS data errors cost realtors, why they happen, and free checks to fix listing data before you submit. Examples use published fine schedules.
targetKeyword: avoid mls fines by correcting listing data errors
intro: To avoid MLS fines by correcting listing data errors, check every field against your board's rulebook before you submit. Then track each deadline, because late-entry fines add up daily. Fines are set locally, so the amounts depend on where you list. This page uses published schedules from Daytona Beach REALTORS and Canopy MLS as examples, and it says where the evidence runs out.
tldr: Each MLS or board sets its own fines. Daytona Beach REALTORS charges $25 per field, per occurrence, for mismatched free-form content.
Deadlines cost more than single typos on that schedule. A late filing can run $100 per listing, per business day.
Check free-form fields, living area, property type, and dates before you hit submit.
A Google Sheets pre-entry check and Mac Text Replacements catch repeat slips. Neither one checks your MLS rules for you.
No national count of MLS fines appears in the sources we opened. Read your own board's current schedule.

blocks.text: What an MLS fine looks like on paper

Each MLS or board sets its own fines. The National Association of REALTORS explains why listing errors happen, but its April 2025 article lists no fine amounts. For concrete numbers, this page uses Daytona Beach REALTORS' published schedule and Canopy MLS's notice on new violations. Your board may use different amounts, so treat these as examples, not as your rule.

rows: Free-form field does not match its field name
$25 per field, per occurrence
A second offense of the same infraction within six months doubles the fine
Listing not filed within 48 hours after all seller signatures
$100 per listing, per business day

blocks.caption: Daytona Beach REALTORS fine schedule, as published on its MLS fines page. The page shows no date.

blocks.text: Canopy MLS takes a different route. Its fines for offer-of-compensation violations, consumer-disclosure failures, and buyer-agreement failures began January 1, 2025, at $100 each. The year before was a warning-only period. Canopy also runs a Listing Data Checker that flags listings with words such as compensation and commission for staff review. If you use those words in your listing text, expect a flag.
Worked example: three small errors on one listing

Say a listing has three free-form fields that do not match their field names. On the Daytona schedule, that is $25 times three, or $75. If the same infraction happens again within six months, the fine doubles to $50 per field, or $150 for the three fields. Now add a late filing. If the listing is entered five business days after the 48-hour window closes, the schedule adds $100 per business day, or $500. The first-offense total is $575. That assumes both infractions apply to one listing and nothing else applies.
Use the same steps to size your own exposure. Start with the schedule for the MLS where you list, not with this example.

items: Download your MLS's fine schedule and save a dated copy to your computer.
List each infraction that applies to the listings you take, such as free-form fields, late filing, and closing data.
Write the unit next to each amount: per field, per day, per listing, or per occurrence.
Count the slips you made in the last six months. Repeats change the math under the Daytona schedule.
Compare the total with the time a second read takes. The fine is the cost you can measure.

blocks.text: Why deadlines cost more than a single mistake

A mismatched field costs $25 at a time on the Daytona schedule. Deadlines cost more, and they keep running. A late filing adds $100 per listing for each business day until it is entered. Missed closing information adds $20 per day, capped at $200 per occurrence. Clear Cooperation carries a $500 first fine and a $1,000 second fine, with no warning period.

The schedule uses two clocks you should track. One starts when all seller signatures are in. The other starts when the property is publicly marketed. Write both dates on the listing paperwork the day you get them. A calendar alert with the time on it is harder to ignore than a note in a folder.

blocks.text: Set up a pre-entry check in Google Sheets

A shared sheet gives you one place to type a listing before you enter it in the MLS. You are not linking to the MLS. You are catching obvious mistakes in your own copy. Dropdowns keep property type and status in your board's exact words.

items: Open a new Google Sheet. In row 1, type a header for each field you check, such as Property type and Status.
Select the Property type column. Choose Data > Data validation > Add rule.
Set the criteria to Dropdown. Type your board's exact category names, one per line.
Under Advanced options, look at If the data is invalid. The default rejects anything off the list. Choose Show a warning if you need room to override on purpose.
Repeat for Status. Keep both lists in one tab so you can update them when the board changes a rule.

blocks.text: The sheet checks only what you type into it. It does not read the MLS, and it does not know your board's rules unless you put them there. Update the lists each time the rulebook changes. A stale list is worse than none, because it looks trustworthy.
Use Text Replacements for approved boilerplate, not facts

Text Replacements on Mac expand a short trigger into a longer phrase. It saves typing. It does not check the phrase against your board's rules. Use it only for text your MLS already approves, such as a standard closing line. Never use it for square footage or dates, because those change per listing.

items: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements.
Click Add. In the Replace column, type a short trigger you will not type by accident.
In the With column, paste the approved text. Read it once against the current rulebook.
To review your list from inside an app, choose Edit > Substitutions > Show Substitutions.

blocks.text: Review the list every few months, and whenever the board changes a rule. Stale boilerplate causes errors that look intentional. A shortcut that worked last year can insert wording your board no longer allows.

Lazur helps with the reading and the typing, not the submitting. It explains a term on screen, points at a field, and walks you through a Sheets menu one click at a time. It does not click buttons, edit files, or enter listing data for you. Every field you submit is still your job.
Mistakes people make with listing data

items: Trusting a county or city record without checking it against the property. NAR warns about this directly.
Reusing last season's remarks template after your board changed a rule.
Treating a one-business-day clock as a suggestion. On the Daytona schedule it carries a fine with no warning period.
Fixing the listing but not logging the slip. Repeats count more under the six-month rule.
Assuming someone else pays the fine. Ask your broker who pays on your listings, because this page does not cover that.
Skipping the check on routine listings. Templates carry old wording most often in the listings you copy.

blocks.text: What we could not verify

No national count of MLS fines appears in the sources we opened. We did not find a study showing how often listing errors happen, or how long they take to fix. We also found no evidence that dropdowns, Text Replacements, or a second read reduce error rates. Those tools make a check easier to run. They do not prove that a check works.
The Daytona fine page shows no date. Schedules change. Read the current version from your board, save a dated copy, and rely on that copy instead of this page.

Privacy and brokerage rules for listing work

Listing data includes seller details and property records. If your brokerage has rules on sharing that data with an AI tool, follow them before you use voice help on a listing. Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

blocks.text: Download the fine schedule and rulebook, add the date to the file name, and keep it in one folder. When a fine notice arrives, you will know which version applied.

faq.question: Is there one national MLS fine schedule?
faq.answer: No. The sources we opened describe local schedules, such as Daytona Beach REALTORS' and Canopy MLS's. Each board sets its own amounts, so check the rulebook for the MLS where you list.

faq.question: Do the Daytona Beach amounts apply to my MLS?
faq.answer: Probably not. Fine schedules differ by board, and the Daytona page shows no date. Use those numbers to understand how a schedule can work, then find your board's current version.

faq.question: What is the fastest way to stop a repeat slip?
faq.answer: Find the step that let the slip through, such as a template or a missing check, and fix it. Then log the slip with the date. Repeats within six months can cost more under the Daytona schedule.

faq.question: Can Lazur check my listing against MLS rules?
faq.answer: No. Lazur can explain a term on screen, point at a field, guide you through a menu, and draft text. It does not check MLS rules for you or enter listing data. Your rulebook is the final check.

faq.question: Does Text Replacements change what the MLS accepts?
faq.answer: No. Text Replacements types text faster. It does not check whether that text meets your board's rules, so review each saved phrase against the current rulebook.

faq.question: Do the Canopy keywords mean a listing will be fined?
faq.answer: Not by themselves. Canopy's Listing Data Checker flags listings that contain words such as compensation and commission for staff review. Read the full Canopy notice to see what happens after a flag.

faq.question: Who pays an MLS fine, the agent or the brokerage?
faq.answer: The sources here do not say how brokerages handle fines. Ask your broker who pays on your listings, and get the answer in writing if it matters to your business.

costs.title: Per-field fines add up fast
costs.text: On the Daytona schedule, each free-form field that does not match its name costs $25 per occurrence. A listing with three bad fields costs $75 on the first offense. The same mistake repeated within six months costs double. The total grows with every field you miss, not just with the listing.

costs.title: Deadline fines grow every day
costs.text: A late filing runs $100 per listing for each business day until it is entered, after the 48-hour window. Missed closing information adds $20 per day, capped at $200 per occurrence. Under Clear Cooperation, a listing missed by one business day of public marketing carries a $500 first fine and a $1,000 second, with no warning.

costs.title: Repeat slips move up the schedule
costs.text: The Daytona schedule doubles a fine for a second offense within six months and triples a third. A fourth or later offense is five times the initial fee. One repeated slip can cost several times what the first one did. Keep a log so you can see the pattern early.

costs.title: Bad data reaches appraisals and pricing
costs.text: NAR says inaccurate MLS data skews search and statistical results. That affects comparative market analyses, broker price opinions, and appraisals. Clients make decisions from those documents. The sources give no dollar figure for that harm, so this page does not put one on it.

costs.title: Time is the cost nobody counts
costs.text: We found no sourced figure for the hours that listing fixes take. Count your own hours for one month. Include the back-and-forth with your MLS office, because people often forget that part.

causes.title: Manual entry and missing details
causes.text: NAR's April 4, 2025 article lists entering data incorrectly and leaving out details as causes of MLS errors. Each copy of the same fact is another chance to mistype it. Retyping the square footage in three places multiplies the risk. Enter each fact once, then copy it from your own sheet.

causes.title: Terms used loosely
causes.text: NAR gives walk-out versus walk-up basement as an example of a misused term. The two words describe different access, and an MLS field may expect one exact choice. Agents often pick the term that sounds closest. Check the definition your board uses, not the one you remember from school or a past listing.

causes.title: Counting space the wrong way
causes.text: NAR lists counting below-grade space as living area as a cause of errors. A finished basement can look like a bedroom or a family room in photos, and it can still fall outside your board's living area rule. Check the definition before you type a number into that field.

causes.title: Trusting public records
causes.text: NAR warns against trusting county or municipal records without verifying them. Public records may not match the house as it stands today. Check each value against the property before you enter it. A record is a starting point, not proof.

causes.title: Templates that outlive the rules
causes.text: Remarks templates, saved text, and copied listings carry old wording forward. A phrase that passed last year can break a rule now. The template does not warn you. Nothing in the copy tells you it is out of date.

causes.title: Deadlines that land in the middle of other work
causes.text: The clocks on the Daytona schedule start from events such as seller signatures and closing. Those events arrive during showings, calls, and offers. If you do not write the deadline down, it slips. A missed date then becomes a fine on the schedule.

fixes.title: Save your board's rulebook and fine schedule
fixes.text: Find the rulebook on your board or MLS website, then ask your MLS office for the current version. Save it as a PDF with the date in the file name. Schedules change, and the Daytona page shows no date. A dated copy tells you which rule applied when you listed the home.

fixes.title: Match each free-form field to its name
fixes.text: On the Daytona schedule, free-form fields such as Remarks, Directions, Street, Legal, Lot Size, and Agent Info must hold content that matches the field name. Before you submit, read each one out loud. Ask whether it says what the field name says. If not, move the text to the right place or delete it.

fixes.title: Run a fresh second read on high-risk fields
fixes.text: Read property type, living area, and dates again after a short break. A fresh read catches what the first one skipped. If someone on your team can check, let them. We found no study that measures how much a second read helps, but it costs little to run.

fixes.title: Put every deadline on a list
fixes.text: Write the clocks on each listing: 48 hours after all seller signatures, one business day after public marketing, and 48 hours after closing. Add them to Apple Reminders or your calendar with an alert. Check the list each morning. Confirm the numbers against your own board's schedule first.

fixes.title: Flag compensation and commission words before you submit
fixes.text: Canopy's Listing Data Checker flags listings that contain words such as compensation and commission for staff review. Search your remarks for those words before you submit. If your board allows them only in certain fields, move them. Ask the MLS office when you are unsure where a phrase belongs.

fixes.title: Keep a slip log
fixes.text: Make a sheet with five columns: date, listing, field, what went wrong, and fix. Add a line each time a check catches a slip or misses one. Under the six-month rule on the Daytona schedule, a repeat costs more, so the log shows you when a pattern forms.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Get the rules in writing
plan.text: Download your board's rulebook and fine schedule. Save a dated PDF. List the free-form fields, the deadlines, and any compensation rules you find in it.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Build the pre-entry sheet
plan.text: Make a Google Sheet with dropdowns for property type and status. Set each one to Show a warning. Use your board's exact category names in the lists.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set up approved shortcuts
plan.text: Add Text Replacements only for boilerplate your MLS approves. Check each phrase against the rulebook, then test it once in a note before you rely on it.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Run the check on live listings
plan.text: Use the sheet and a field-by-field read on every listing you submit. Log each slip with the date, the field, and the fix you made.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review the log and the clocks
plan.text: Look for repeats in the log. Confirm every open listing has its deadlines on your calendar. Email your MLS office about any field you cannot match to a rule.
